Shrimp With Chorizo-Tomato Sauce

The secret to this smoky shrimp dinner is turning Spanish chorizo into the sauce.

By
Amanda Luchtel
Amanda Luchtel
Amanda Luchtel is a private chef, food writer and editor, recipe developer, and content creator based in New England. As a former fine-dining and private chef, she understands the impact food has on our daily lives. Over the years, she has developed a passion for seasonal and regional cooking.
Serious Eats' Editorial Guidelines
Published on July 24, 2026
In This Recipe
View All
In This Article
  • Selecting and Preparing the Chorizo
  • The Blending Step That Upgrades the Sauce
  • How to Keep the Shrimp Tender
  • Blending the chorizo, tomatoes, and chipotles after cooking creates a fully emulsified sauce, dispersing fat and flavor evenly so it clings to the shrimp instead of separating.
  • Cooking the shrimp separately over high heat ensures they stay tender. 

At first glance, this might look like a simple shrimp-and-chorizo skillet dinner. But what makes this version special is the sauce. Instead of serving the shrimp alongside slices of smoky Spanish chorizo, the sausage is simmered with tomatoes, garlic, chipotles, and stock, then blended into a smooth, savory sauce that coats every shrimp.

I first made a version of the dish while working at Charlie Palmer at the Joule Hotel in Dallas, Texas. The restaurant preparation was more involved, but the combination stuck with me. Sweet shrimp and smoky chorizo are a natural pairing, and turning the chorizo into the backbone of the sauce creates a dish far more interesting than the ingredient list suggests.

Selecting and Preparing the Chorizo

This recipe depends on Spanish-style chorizo, which is different from fresh Mexican version. Spanish chorizo is cured, fermented, and heavily seasoned with smoked paprika, giving it a firm texture and concentrated flavor.

As it cooks, the sausage releases paprika-rich fat that becomes the foundation of the sauce. Onion and garlic soften in that flavorful fat, while tomatoes and chipotles in adobo add sweetness, acidity, and smoky heat. A splash of white wine dissolves the flavorful browned bits that form on the bottom of the pan, and reducing the stock concentrates everything into a savory base.

The Blending Step That Upgrades the Sauce

Once the chorizo mixture has simmered and reduced, pureeing it transforms the texture from a chunky braise into a smooth, cohesive sauce. More importantly, blending disperses the rendered chorizo fat throughout the liquid, creating an emulsion that helps the sauce cling to the shrimp rather than separate.

The result is a thick sauce that’s smoky, savory, and lightly spicy. Each bite delivers a balanced combination of chorizo, tomato, garlic, and chile.

How to Keep the Shrimp Tender

At the restaurant, the shrimp were grilled before being finished in the sauce, adding a subtle char and another layer of smokiness. At home, a hot skillet delivers a similar flavor with less fuss.

Searing the shrimp until lightly browned adds an important layer of flavor, one that’s much more complex and helps marry the shrimp with the smoky heat of the sauce. As soon as they’ve developed that golden exterior and have just turned opaque, they go into the sauce for a very brief simmer to finish cooking.

A final pat of butter swirled in off the heat gives the sauce a glossy finish and helps round out some of the chipotle heat. Lemon juice and cilantro, meanwhile, provide a fresh contrast to the rich, smoky base.

Served with plenty of crusty bread for swiping through the sauce, it’s a dish that’s equally at home as a casual weeknight dinner or the centerpiece of a tapas-style spread.

June, 2026

Prep Time:
5 mins
Cook Time:
25 mins
Total Time:
30 mins
Servings:
4 to 6
Keep Screen Awake

Ingredients

  • 2 pounds extra-large shrimp, peeled, deveined, and tails removed (see notes)

  • 5 medium cloves garlic, 2 minced and 3 smashed, divided

  • 1 1/2 teaspoons (6 g) Diamond Crystal kosher salt; for table salt, use about half as much by volume or the same weight, divided

  • 3/4 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper

  • 4 tablespoons (60 ml) extra-virgin olive oil, divided

  • 4 ounces Spanish dry-cured chorizo, casing removed, quartered lengthwise, and cut into 1/4-inch pieces

  • 1 small yellow onion (4 ounces; 113 g), chopped (about 3/4 cup)

  • 2 plum tomatoes, cored and chopped (about 1 cup)

  • 1 to 2 canned chipotles in adobo (see notes)

  • 1/2 cup (120 ml) dry white wine or dry sherry (see notes)

  • 3 cups (720 ml) homemade chicken stock or store-bought low-sodium chicken broth

  • 4 tablespoons (57 g) unsalted butter, cut into four pieces

  • 1 tablespoon (15 ml) fresh lemon juice

  • 1/4 cup roughly chopped fresh cilantro leaves

  • Crusty bread, for serving

Directions

  1. In a medium bowl, toss shrimp, 2 minced garlic cloves, 1 teaspoon kosher salt, and pepper to combine; set aside.

  2. In a 12-inch stainless steel skillet, heat 2 tablespoons oil over medium heat until shimmering. Add chorizo, onion, and remaining 3 smashed garlic cloves, and cook until onion is softened and beginning to brown, 4 to 5 minutes. Add tomatoes, chipotle in adobo, and remaining 1/2 teaspoon kosher salt and cook until tomato begins to break down and a browned layer begins to form on the bottom of the pot, 3 to 4 minutes.

  3. Add wine and cook until reduced by half, scraping up the browned bits on bottom of skillet, about 2 minutes. Add chicken stock or broth. Increase heat to medium-high and bring to a vigorous simmer. Simmer until reduced by half (about 2 1/4 cups), 10 to 12 minutes.

  4. Carefully transfer chorizo mixture to a blender and process on high until smooth, 2 to 3 minutes, scraping down sides of blender jar as needed. Rinse and dry the skillet.

  5. Return now-clean skillet to medium-high heat and heat remaining 2 tablespoons oil in skillet until just smoking. Add shrimp and cook, stirring occasionally, until shrimp are opaque and just cooked through, 3 to 4 minutes.

  6. Add sauce and bring to a simmer, about 30 seconds. Off heat, stir in butter and lemon juice until butter is melted. Season with salt and pepper to taste. Sprinkle with cilantro and serve with crusty bread. 

Special Equipment

12-inch stainless steel skillet, wooden spoon, blender

Notes

While fish counters often sell shrimp as “medium” or “large,” the industry usually sizes them by count per pound. For this recipe, shrimp in the 21/25 or 26/30 range—roughly medium to medium-large—work well.

Sherry can be substituted for white wine to add a more oaky, nutty flavor, if desired. 

1 1/2 teaspoons smoked paprika and 1/2 teaspoon cayenne pepper can be substituted for chipotle in adobo. 

Make-Ahead and Storage

The sauce can be made up to 2 days ahead. To finish, season the shrimp and let sit for 15 to 20 minutes. Meanwhile, rewarm the sauce in a small saucepan, then continue to step 5.
